newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: SLOVAK FINMIN MULLS FOREIGNER T-BILL PARTICIPATION.
newsitem.headline: SLOVAK FINMIN MULLS FOREIGNER T-BILL PARTICIPATION.

text.p: The Slovak Finance Ministry on Monday said it may allow foreign investors access to buying treasury bills to help refinance the state budget deficit.
"Until now we did not need foreign participants, but now we are considering allowing them to buy our T-bills," Juraj Macejka, head of the ministry's department of state account, told Reuters.
Current legislation allows foreigners to buy state bonds, but the purchase of T-bills requires prior finance ministry approval, and to date no foreigners have purchased the paper.
Macejka declined to disclose any possible date for such a move, saying that "further discussion would be premature as everything is in the drawing board stage".

He said allowing foreign participation in T-bill auctions would depend "on the liquidity of domestic commercial banks, their ability to absorb the amount of planned state securities and interest rates on the interbank money market."
"But of course we will have to discuss such a move with our agent in T-bill auctions, the central bank, mainly from the point of view of monetary policy," Macejka added.
The Slovak parliament last month approved a 1997 budget that sees a 36.9 billion crown deficit after a planned 1996 deficit of 27 billion crowns.
The 1997 state budget says that the finance ministry plans to issue an overall amount of 70 billion crowns in state securities this year to finance last year's and this year's budget deficits.
Slovak money market analysts welcomed the move saying they expected foreig demand for the paper because of its high yield, adding the move could also increase market liquidity.
"I think there will be big foreign interest in T-bills, as the current yields are very attractive," said Martin Hrozany, chief dealer at Slovenska Sporitelna.
"If foreign banks buy enough T-bills, it could lead to a decline in interbank interest rates and to higher liquidity in the banking sector within two to-three-month period."
At the ministry's last auction of four-week T-bills on January 8, the average yield rose to 13.64 percent from 12.55 percent in the last auction of similar bills on December 30.

But the finance ministry, which uses T-bills and domestic state bonds as its main tools to refinance the deficit, has said current yield on treasury bills was high and that it was not prepared to allow them to rise further.

Slovak short-term interbank money market rates continued to rise to a bid range of 20-24 percent on Monday, and dealers said they expected them to rise even further higher as the sector lacks sufficient liquidity ahead of Wednesday's minimum reserve deadline.
